abstract: Automatically predicting RNA 3D structure from sequence remains an unsolved challenge in biology and biotechnology. Here, we describe a Kaggle code competition engaging over 1700 teams and 43 previously unreleased structures to tackle this challenge. The top three submitted algorithms achieved scores within statistical error of the winners of the recent CASP16 competition. Unexpectedly, the top Kaggle strategy involved a pipeline for discovering 3D templates, without the use of deep learning. We integrated this template-modeling pipeline and other Kaggle strategies to develop a single model RNAPro that retrospectively outperformed individual Kaggle models on the same test set. These results suggest a growing importance of template-based modeling in RNA structure prediction.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This preprint shows early but meaningful uptake in a fast-moving computational biology niche: it is already being used in teaching-adjacent public discussion and has a documented downstream reuse in the literature. The record also shows one YouTube video from the CASP RNA SIG explicitly linking the paper, and one Europe PMC article mention, while citation counts remain very small at this stage.

Full narrative

The article reports a Kaggle code competition designed to test RNA 3D structure prediction using 43 previously unreleased structures and more than 1,700 teams. Its central result is notable for the method that emerged strongest in the competition: rather than relying on deep learning, the top-performing strategy was a pipeline for discovering 3D templates. That finding gives the paper a clear methodological hook for researchers working on RNA folding, structure search, and benchmark design.

The surrounding impact record is still early, but it is not empty. OpenAlex shows two citations in 2026, including follow-on work in Nature Protocols on the trRosettaRNA server and a Chemical Science article discussing black-box data in biomedicine and AI. Scite also records four mentions, which is consistent with a paper that is being noticed in adjacent conversations even before a substantial citation base has accumulated.

There is also a small but concrete signal of reuse and community circulation. The teaching-adoption data include a CASP RNA SIG YouTube video that explicitly links the paper in its metadata or description, suggesting that the work is already being introduced to a specialist audience. In addition, the reuse graph shows one documented downstream reuse, indicating that the paper is being referenced in structured scholarly or biomedical indexing rather than remaining purely a standalone preprint.

Overall, the record points to an influential methods paper in the making: strongly aligned with RNA structure prediction, visible in a specialist competition community, and beginning to move into downstream literature and instructional contexts. The evidence is still sparse, so the safest reading is that this work has early adoption and emerging reuse, with its longer-term scholarly influence still unfolding.
